displayQuote: When the Okies left Oklahoma and moved to California, they raised the average intelligence level in both states

meta.title: Who really said "When the Okies left Oklahoma and moved to California, they raised the average intelligence level in both states"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Will Rogers died in 1935. The Okie IQ joke is documented from 1939, first credited to him in 1970, and Quote Investigator finds no source in his work.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the Okies left Oklahoma and moved to California, they raised the average intelligence level in both states'?
meta.ogDescription: Documented in print from 1939 — years after Rogers died — and first pinned on him in 1970. Quote Investigator finds no match in his writings.

answer.label: Not Will Rogers — an anonymous newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: Credited to Will Rogers (1879–1935) only from 1970 · true originator unknown
answer.sourceLine: Will Rogers died in 1935, and Quote Investigator ↗ could find no match for this quip anywhere in his writings. The joke first appears in print in April 1939 — after Rogers was already dead, and told about two Mississippi counties rather than Okies. It attaches to the Okie migration by January 1955, and Rogers’s name is first attached to it in February 1970, when Oklahoma Governor Dewey F. Bartlett told a Long Beach audience “I like what Will Rogers once said.” QI’s verdict is that Rogers probably did not employ this joke.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None — no match located in his columns, telegrams or broadcasts
“The Jackson Go-Round” by Herbert L. Carver, McComb Daily Journal (Mississippi), 6 April 1939, p. 5
The Seminole Producer (Seminole, Oklahoma), 5 January 1955, p. 6 — industrialist Harry Woodhead, quoted by Leland Gourley
Los Angeles Times, 6 February 1970 — Governor Dewey F. Bartlett, speaking in Long Beach

source.excerpt: “Hundreds of thousands of Okies migrated to California during the dust bowl days,” Woodhead relates. “Right after this, they made a survey and found the I. Q. of both states had been raised considerably.”
trail: The joke is older than its Okie form. The earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ located ran in the McComb Daily Journal of Mississippi on 6 April 1939, in a column by Herbert L. Carver: a man “moved from one south Mississippi county to another, and when he did he raised the intelligence level of both counties.” QI conjectures that Carver was already repeating an existing quip.

It then travelled through the 1940s and 1950s attached to whoever was handy — a preacher going to Arkansas (1941), two arguing farmers in The Rotarian (1942), a student transferring from Michigan to Ohio State (1944), a man moving from Nebraska to Kansas (1955), an Oklahoman moving to Texas (1962) — each transcribed with a full citation by Quote Investigator ↗.

Rogers’s name enters in 1970, and only there. Governor Dewey F. Bartlett had told the joke unattributed in September 1969; on 6 February 1970 the Los Angeles Times reported him prefacing it with “I like what Will Rogers once said,” and in 1975 he credited Rogers again, this time with a Texas variant, in testimony to a U.S. Senate committee Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote offers the attribution no help either: its Will Rogers page lists the line in neither its sourced quotations nor its misattributed section Wikiquote: Will Rogers ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest version tied to the Okie migration that Quote Investigator located — and it is not Will Rogers speaking. It is the industrialist Harry Woodhead, quoted in an Oklahoma newspaper in January 1955, long after Rogers’s death, telling a joke whose earliest documented form (1939) had nothing to do with Oklahoma at all.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted here. The sentence in circulation matches none of the dated instances on record, so there is no identifiable author, work or first-publication date against which copyright could be assessed — and the earliest documented ancestor, a 1939 newspaper column, is neither this wording nor Will Rogers’s. Treat the line as an anonymous saying of unestablished origin rather than as public-domain Rogers material.

author.name: Will Rogers
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Will Rogers
author.metaLine: 1879–1935 · American humorist, newspaper columnist and film star
author.bio: Will Rogers was a trick roper from Indian Territory — born near Oologah in 1879 — who became the most quoted American of his day: more than 4,000 nationally syndicated newspaper columns, 71 films, and a Sunday radio show for Gulf Oil, all built on plainspoken jokes about the news. He died on 15 August 1935, when Wiley Post’s plane crashed in Alaska Territory, and that date is what settles this quote: the joke is not documented anywhere in print until 1939. His name became a magnet for orphaned one-liners precisely because homespun American wit was the thing he sold — an Oklahoma joke about Okies sounds like him, which is exactly why it stuck.

Rogers died in August 1935; the joke is documented in print from April 1939 (told about two Mississippi counties), reached the Okie migration by January 1955, and was first credited to Rogers in February 1970. misattribution.heading: The misattribution, step by step
misattribution.intro: This is a joke that travelled for three decades before anyone put a famous name on it. The name it eventually got was the most plausible one available — Oklahoma’s own humorist, dead since 1935 and therefore in no position to deny it.

items.why: Rogers died on 15 August 1935. The first documented time anyone put this joke in his mouth was 6 February 1970, when Oklahoma Governor Dewey F. Bartlett told a Town Hall of California gathering in Long Beach, “I like what Will Rogers once said: When the Okies migrated to California, it raised the I.Q. in both states.” Bartlett had used the very same joke the previous September, reported in the Sequoyah County Times, with no attribution to anyone at all Quote Investigator ↗.

None of the dated instances Quote Investigator transcribes — 1939, 1941, 1942, 1944, 1952, 1955, 1957, 1959, 1962, 1969, 1970 — uses the polished sentence that circulates today. The earliest of all, in the McComb Daily Journal of Mississippi on 6 April 1939, is about one man moving between two Mississippi counties; the earliest Okie version, from January 1955, has a survey finding “the I. Q. of both states had been raised considerably” Quote Investigator ↗.

Roy B. Zuck’s The Speaker’s Quote Book printed it flatly under Rogers’s name in a first-person form he is not documented using — “When I moved from Oklahoma to California the IQ of both states went up” — which is how an unsourced platform joke turns into a reference-book fact Quote Investigator ↗.

The identical gag is credited to New Zealand Prime Minister Robert Muldoon, about New Zealanders moving to Australia; a journalist reported hearing him tell it in The Sydney Morning Herald in 1990, and the Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (2008) files it under his name as “attributed.” Muldoon really did tell it — but, as with Rogers, the joke was old long before he got to it Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that the quips credited to Rogers and to Muldoon belong to “an evolving family of expressions which was initiated by 1939” — and that Will Rogers probably did not employ this joke Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: The joke that became a medical term
lead: The Dust Bowl migration is the thing this joke is standing on. Through the mid-1930s hundreds of thousands of farming families left the Great Plains and Southwest for California, and Californians began calling all of them “Okies” whether or not they came from Oklahoma — a label that started as an insult and only later got reclaimed as a badge of honour Okie ↗. The gag insults both ends of the road at once, which is why an Oklahoma governor could tell it about his own state and still get a laugh.

Then it had a second life nobody expected. In 1985 the clinician Alvan Feinstein and colleagues borrowed the line to name a real statistical trap in cancer staging: better scanning moved patients who looked healthy out of the ‘good’ stage and into the ‘bad’ one, so survival figures improved in both groups while no individual patient did any better. They called it the Will Rogers phenomenon, and the name stuck in medicine Will Rogers phenomenon ↗.
detailsBody: The paper is Alvan R. Feinstein, Daniel M. Sosin and Carolyn K. Wells, “The Will Rogers phenomenon. Stage migration and new diagnostic techniques as a source of misleading statistics for survival in cancer,” New England Journal of Medicine 312, no. 25 (20 June 1985): 1604–8 PubMed record ↗.

The mechanism is the same as the joke’s: move members from one group to another whose average they sit between, and both averages rise even though nothing about the members themselves changed. That is a genuinely useful idea, which is part of why the misattribution has proved so durable — the name now travels through medical literature, not just through quotation books.
context.pull: A joke nobody can source became a technical term in oncology — under the name of a man who is not documented ever telling it.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI dates the earliest known instance to Herbert L. Carver's column in the McComb Daily Journal, 6 April 1939 (a man moving between two south Mississippi counties); the earliest Okie-specific version to Harry Woodhead in The Seminole Producer, 5 January 1955; Bartlett's unattributed use to the Sequoyah County Times, 11 September 1969; the first credit to Will Rogers to the Los Angeles Times, 6 February 1970; a further Rogers credit in Bartlett's 1975 Senate testimony; the Speaker's Quote Book entry (1997); the Muldoon report in the Sydney Morning Herald (1990) and the Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations (2008). QI concludes the quips belong to 'an evolving family of expressions which was initiated by 1939' and that 'Will Rogers probably did not employ this joke.'

The article attributes the quip to Will Rogers, states that clinician Alvan Feinstein coined the term 'Will Rogers phenomenon' in 1985, and notes the quotation was first attributed to native Oklahoman Rogers decades after his death, with versions of the same joke circulating at least 15 years before it can be linked to Okies.
Wikiquote's Will Rogers page has a Misattributed section, and it does not list the Okies / Oklahoma / California intelligence quote in that section or anywhere else on the page.

Will Rogers was born 4 November 1879 near Oologah, Indian Territory, and died 15 August 1935 in the crash of Wiley Post's plane in Alaska Territory; he wrote more than 4,000 nationally syndicated newspaper columns, made 71 films, and broadcast for Gulf Oil from 1929 to 1935.

PubMed record PMID 4000199 is Feinstein AR, Sosin DM, Wells CK, 'The Will Rogers phenomenon. Stage migration and new diagnostic techniques as a source of misleading statistics for survival in cancer,' New England Journal of Medicine, 20 June 1985, 312(25):1604-8. (Bibliographic fields confirmed via the NCBI E-utilities esummary API for this same PMID; the HTML page itself returned a cookie interstitial to the fetcher.)

'Okie' denotes a person identified with Oklahoma; during the mid-1930s Dust Bowl large numbers of farmers migrated from the Great Plains and Southwest to California, and Californians began calling all migrants by that name even though many newcomers were not actually Oklahomans - a pejorative later reclaimed as a badge of honour.

The Will Rogers Memorial Museum's Writings page describes his daily telegrams (syndicated in over 500 newspapers from July 1926 until his death in August 1935) and his weekly articles, and offers downloadable PDF volumes of his writings.
